title: Europe wrestles with impact of historic regional gains for Germany’s AfD
description: "Seismic", "a socio-political earthquake", "a watershed moment for Germany".This was how political analysts and many media outlets described the stunn
body: "Seismic", "a socio-political earthquake", "a watershed moment for Germany".This was how political analysts and many media outlets described the stunning victory of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in local elections in Germany on Sunday. Is that an exaggeration?Saxony-Anhalt is one of the smallest of massive Germany's 16 regions. It boasts a mere 1.7m out of 59m eligible voters nationwide. How significant can its political sentiments be, especially since the AfD narrowly failed to win an outright majority?The answer: Very significant.First and foremost, at home in Germany.The vote may have been regional but it impacts at national level. The AfD landslide piles even more pressure on the already beleaguered centrist coalition government in Berlin. It may prove to be the nail in the political coffin of Germany's deeply unpopular conservative Chancellor, Friedrich Merz. He had promised to slash the AfD's popularity.These political woes will further weaken and distract Germany, the EU's most powerful player, at a time of continental crisis - as Europe struggles to contain Russian aggression, US President Donald Trump's tariff tantrums and the economic threat from China.The Saxony-Anhalt result also provokes soul-searching throughout Germany, where the Nazi past still looms large. This is the first outstanding electoral landslide for a hard-right nationalist party - giving it a real shot at governing, in this case, at regional level - since the fall of the Third Reich in 1945.The German authorities have labelled the AfD, in part, anti-democratic and a number of regional factions of the party, including Saxony-Anhalt, far-right extremist.The AfD is well-known to be particularly popular in east Germany but it is now also polling as the biggest political party nationwide.Germany's political mainstream has failed voters, it would seem. What does Europe's biggest single economy, its most populous nation not counting Russia, do now?Tiny Saxony-Anhalt is causing waves outside Germany, too.None other than the US president swiftly posted the Saxony-Anhalt exit poll on his Truth Social platform on Sunday.The AfD's anti-immigration, anti-woke, "Germany for Germans" message chimes closely with Donald Trump's Maga [Make America Great Again] missive. Along with a number of other nationalist parties in Europe, the AfD borrows heavily from the Trump playbook - undermining mainstream media, questioning the neutrality of judges and promising to "make Germany great again".Interesting to note though - the US president is rarely name-checked on the campaign trail in Europe. Politicians are keenly aware just how unpopular he is amongst voters.Hot on Donald Trump's social media heels on Sunday night was the influential Russian businessman Kirill Dmitriev, CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund. He declared the AfD result "historic", Germany's national government "discredited" and the German chancellor "humiliated", comparing Friedrich Merz to the UK's not-long-gone Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, who felt forced to resign this summer.What interest might Russia have in German regional elections, you might ask, and what was Dmitriev's dig at the UK all about?The German government is the largest single donor to Ukraine and the UK is known to have provided Kyiv with missiles used to strike inside Russian territory. This has deeply angered Moscow.The AfD, by comparison, is pretty pro-Russia. It wants to stop sending military aid to Ukraine, halt sanctions against Moscow and start buying much cheaper Russian energy again. Energy-hungry German industry suffered a huge economic blow after the country halted Russian energy imports, following Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.The AfD's softly-softly approach to Russia has another appeal in Germany's east, which remains far poorer than the west. This, despite Germany spending between 2.3 and 3tn (£2tn-£2.6tn) - depending on reports and whether inflation is taken into account - to help integrate the former Communist part of the country after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.Saxony-Anhalt is Germany's poorest region and there, as in much of east Germany, you often encounter what's known as "Ostalgie" amongst voters; essentially "nostalgia in the east" for comparatively more stable times under Communism.Also watching the Saxony-Anhalt election closely was the European Union. The next 12 months is bumper election season across the EU. Ballots are expected in key nations France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Brussels fears more "extreme" parties, left but particularly right of the political spectrum, may benefit across the board.The leader of Spain's nationalist Vox party, Santiago Abascal, posted on X on Sunday that the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt was " a great hope for Germany and for Europe".By contrast, France's Europe Minister, Benjamin Haddad, an ally of centrist President Emmanuel Macron, warned "this is a serious moment in Europe, seeing the far-right win in a regional election in Germany".Neither the AfD, nor other European parties labelled "extreme right" or "hard right", accept the label. They also differ from one another in tone and party programme. France's National Rally under Marine Le Pen kicked the AfD out of its grouping in the European Parliament two years ago, for being too "radical". What the parties do tend to share, however, is an anti-immigration platform and strong nationalist messaging. And that really worries the EU.Whether it is a rallying cry for "Germany First" or "Italy First" or "France for the French!", the concern in Brussels is that the rise of nationalist parties strains European cohesion at a time when outside events demand it more than ever.Nationalist parties like the AfD or Italy's League Party tend to be deeply Eurosceptic, but Brussels says Europe needs to stand united to counter Donald Trump's bullying, for example, or to effectively protect European business against China's goods dumping.Europe's defence establishment also warns that fractures in European sanctions against Russia or countries going tepid on Nato membership (as you see in Marine Le Pen's National Rally for example, or Germany's AfD) just emboldens Moscow.Security chiefs say nations must stick together to stop Russia in Ukraine, otherwise the Kremlin will be tempted to attack inside Nato, such as the Baltic states.The thing is, Europe's voters are very aware of these outside threats and the impact they have at home. They worry about the impact of wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, about crumbling health services at home and dwindling economic security for themselves and their families. Uncontrolled immigration and safety on the streets are huge concerns, too.And this is where the significance of the Saxony-Anhalt vote shines bright - a flashing red warning to traditional political parties, but also to institutions across Europe like the judiciary and security services. Those the AfD dismisses as the self-interested "Establishment".Voters on this continent feel lost and let down by parties they have supported over and again for decades. Looking right or left now at election time does not mean they have all suddenly become extremist.The AfD campaign slogan in Saxony-Anhalt was an upbeat "Anything is Possible!" - plus a promise to make Germans feel proud of their country again. Till now untried and untested in government, people seem increasingly willing to give them a go.

schema.headline: Europe wrestles with impact of historic regional gains for Germany’s AfD

title: The £70 refund letter that isn't a scam
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentYou may be among the one million people, mostly women, who will receive letters explaining how
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentYou may be among the one million people, mostly women, who will receive letters explaining how you are eligible for top-up pension payments - and it's not a scam.Those entitled are low earners who have missed out on the money because of the way their pension is administered.HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) will write to people over the next few months, explaining how to receive the payment. Typically they will be due £70, but that may vary considerably depending on their circumstances.Anyone eligible will be contacted automatically but, if you receive a letter, there are various checks you can do to ensure the letter is genuine so you don't get hoodwinked.What's the letter about?When you pay into a pension, the government allows some of the money that would otherwise have been paid in tax to go towards your pension instead. This is known as tax relief, external.For relatively complicated reasons, some low earners whose employer used what's known as a Net Pay Arrangement pension scheme received less than those whose pension was administered through a Relief at Source scheme.Employees have no control over the type of scheme that's used, so the government has decided to top up those who have missed out, through what's called a low earner's pension payment.Typically, they would have earned close to, but not more than, £12,570 a year (the starting point for paying income tax).Top-up payments will initially be paid for the 2024-25 tax year, with automated payments subsequently kicking in for later years.  How can I check the letter is for real?Customers don't need to apply. If eligible, you'll be sent information by HMRC - the UK's tax authority - in a letter or through your online personal tax account, external.HMRC will not text, email or call you about it. If you receive such a call or message, it is a scam. Also, it will never ask you to transfer money, or ask for PIN codes or passwords.Other ways to check contact is smooth and genuine include:Making sure HMRC has your latest addressSearching Gov.uk for "check if a letter you've received from HMRC is genuine", and look for "Low Earner's Pension Payment"HMRC also has advice on spotting a scam, externalCustomers will be asked to provide their bank details through their personal tax account. Customers who are digitally excluded will be able to phone HMRC to accept their payment instead"We know some people may be cautious about unexpected contact, which is why we provide clear information about what to expect and how to verify the contact is genuine," said a HMRC spokesman."Customers can check a letter is genuine on Gov.uk and should only respond via official HMRC channels."Is everyone expected to get paid?Sir Steve Webb, partner at pensions consultancy LCP and a former pensions minister, said he was shocked at how few people the government expected to actually receive the payment.The government has estimated the cost of the project to be much lower than if everyone who was eligible took up the payment."The process of getting these payments to the right people is going to be incredibly painful and there is a real risk of huge non take-up," he said.  "It is vital that communications are effective to make sure that people get the money to which they are entitled."HMRC says it will run an awareness campaign using social media and other channels.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: The £70 refund letter that isn't a scam

title: Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school
description: As the new school year begins in Austria, a law banning headscarves in schools for girls under 14 has gone into force.The law forbids "traditional Mus
body: As the new school year begins in Austria, a law banning headscarves in schools for girls under 14 has gone into force.The law forbids "traditional Muslim" head coverings, such as hijabs or burkas, in public and private schools across the country.Integration Minister Claudia Bauer, from the conservative People's Party (ÖVP), says the headscarf is "a sign of oppression and a means of controlling girls from the earliest childhood".But critics say the new law is fuelling anti-Muslim feeling in the country and could be unconstitutional.The law was brought in by the conservative-led coalition of three centrist parties, the ÖVP, the Social Democrats (SPÖ) and the liberal Neos. They say the law is a "clear commitment to gender equality" and is intended to protect the rights of young girls.Carla Amina Baghajati, from the official Islamic Community in Austria (IGGÖ), told the BBC that the organisation "firmly opposes the ban"."We believe it unjustifiably restricts the fundamental right to freedom of religion and disproportionately affects Muslim girls," she said."Rather than protecting children, it singles out a specific religious practice and risks excluding the very children it claims to support."The IGGÖ said it would support legal challenges by girls and their families "who believe that their fundamental rights are being infringed" and who wished to bring their cases before the Constitutional Court. The court struck down a previous ban on headscarves in primary schools in 2020 on the basis that it contravened the principle of Austria's religious neutrality.Teachers are expected to enforce the new ban if they see a child wearing a headscarf by holding a series of talks with the student and their legal guardians.If there are repeated violations, child services must be notified and as a last resort, guardians could face fines of up to €800 (£685).Some teachers have expressed concerns about having to enforce the ban.The Green Party's Sigi Maurer accused Education Minister Christoph Wiederkehr, from the liberal NEOS, of "creating new conflicts and offloading them onto the teachers".She said teachers were "already under enormous strain" and that Wiederkehr wanted to "foist the role of police officers onto them" on top of their other duties.The opposition far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) says the current ban doesn't go far enough. It is calling for a general prohibition on headscarves and face coverings in schools for students and teachers alike.The FPÖ's Ricarda Berger said there was "no place for political Islam in Austria, and certainly not in our schools".Austria's Chancellor Christian Stocker, leader of the ÖVP, recently called for a constitutional ban on political Islam, telling Austrian public broadcaster ORF he did not "want to live in an Islamic state".In France there has been a ban on wearing any conspicuous religious symbols, including headscarves, turbans and kippas, in schools for more than 20 years.The Austrian law differs from French legislation in that it specifically targets head coverings worn by Muslim women.Austria, like several other European countries including France, Belgium and Denmark, bans the full face veil (niqabs or burkas) in public.Baghajati said the IGGÖ was concerned about "a troubling trend" across Europe "in which complex social challenges are reduced to symbolic measures aimed at minority groups.""Such approaches may generate political attention, but they rarely solve the underlying problems," she said.

schema.headline: Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school

title: Kyiv air raid alerts at record high as Russia launches round the clock strikes
description: Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, according to BBC Verify analysis of governme
body: Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, according to BBC Verify analysis of government figures.Most air attacks used to come at night but Russia's new tactic of striking Ukraine's capital during the day is causing huge disruption to schools and businesses.The round the clock attacks have forced people to head for shelter as many as 13 times a day, with air raid alerts lasting from a few minutes to nearly four and a half hours.Residents in Kyiv are struggling to adapt to this new reality, adding to existing stress and anxiety. The alerts force pupils to leave their classrooms and workers their offices and leave commuters struggling to get home as overland trains stop.This has forced the government to plan a new, two-tier warning system that allows people to carry on working, travelling and studying depending on the scale of the threat.There was a brief pause in attacks on Kyiv over the weekend while US envoys were in town for talks about trying to end the war. But analysis of figures from the state-owned app Kyiv digital shows that since the round-the-clock Russian attacks began at the end of August, air raid sirens have sounded across Kyiv's skies on average 10 times a day.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has held an emergency meeting with ministers and commanders to work out how to produce new high-speed missiles that can intercept the faster Russian drones."You can all see that the Russians have changed the tactics of their strikes against Ukraine and, since August, have been terrorising our people, our cities and our villages far more intensely," the president said.Diplomats say the risk is that Russia will manufacture its fast attack drones more quickly than Ukraine can develop a new generation of interceptors. Some military sources say this threat could become far greater than Russia's ballistic missiles which have largely overcome Ukraine's depleted Patriot defences.Ukraine uses warplanes, anti-aircraft guns and shoulder-launched missiles to try to bring down the jet-powered drones.But Yurii Ihnat, spokesman for the Ukrainian Air Force, said only about 60 percent of the drones were being shot down and they needed new interceptors to tackle the threat. "The task now is to make them faster and equip them with specialised guidance systems so that they can shoot down jet-powered UAVs, the jet-powered Shaheds," he said."The key issue really is having guidance systems, because that is one of the crucial elements. It is not enough for the interceptor simply to fly fast — it has to hit the target. That is very important."Analysts say Russia's aim is not only to weaken Kyiv's morale but also damage Ukraine's economy by targeting businesses and warehouses.The alerts are also disrupting the start of the new academic year and forcing school children to leave their classrooms throughout the day.When another air raid began, some students at the Drahomanov Ukrainian State University in central Kyiv headed underground; others stayed chatting on the street, such is the normality of these alerts.Diana, a student teacher, said she did not sleep well at night and her schedule was disrupted during the day. "Sometimes it is hard because most of the day I need to go to safe places, like the metro or somewhere underground," she said. "It's a terrible time, but thank God we are alive. We go day by day."Ihor, studying to become a chemistry teacher, said he was used to the alerts after many years of war but life was still hard. "We are annoyed by the sirens because they are constant," he said. "It destroys the quality of our education… We cannot study normally."After a drone attack in a residential part of central Kyiv, students from a nearby school were evacuated for fear of explosions or a secondary, so-called "double-tap" attack.Sophia, 17, told us it was very sad but this is what life was like now. "It's a little bit scary to live here in Kyiv," she said. "It's very difficult." The interview was then interrupted by another siren. "We need to go," she said. "It is very dangerous for you to stand in the streets. Maybe we can have a second detonation."

schema.headline: Kyiv air raid alerts at record high as Russia launches round the clock strikes

title: Germany's far-right AfD hails big victory in east, but falls short of majority
description: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has won a decisive victory in Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of mainstream rivals.But
body: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has won a decisive victory in Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of mainstream rivals.But preliminary results show it has fallen short of an outright majority needed to govern alone, with 43.8% of the vote to the conservative CDU's 17.2%, and tricky negotiations on who will run the state lie ahead.AfD's charismatic leader in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, said it was "sensational" and the party had won a mandate to govern.No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing, local education and culture.Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.He along with joint national leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla were overjoyed as exit polls revealed they were on track to score more than double the party's result in 2021.Commentators and political opponents called the victory a watershed and break with the past. Main TV channel Das Erste cancelled its legendary crime drama Tatort to focus on what the result meant."This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the German TV projection on his Truth Social platform, and then Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD". Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference.Polish centre-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk saw the result very differently, saying "in Poland only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD".A crowd of supporters at the AfD election night party HQ erupted in cheers as the projections came up on the screen.A short while later, people burst into singing Germany's national anthem."We have made history in this state," Siegmund said. His opposite number in the CDU, Sven Schulze, conceded victory as he watched the conservative vote slump by more than half on the previous election."This was an extremely tough and intensive election campaign," said Schulze, adding that his party would have to deal with the result.Germany's centre-left SPD described the outcome as "truly dramatic" and national leader Lars Klingbeil, whose party is in government nationally with the CDU, described the outcome as a "signal to Berlin" and he was adamant that they would hear it.The anti-migration AfD stands for Alternative für Deutschland. It has not only dominated the election campaign, it is emerging as the dominant force in the result and its supporters believe they are on the march.Turnout in Saxony-Anhalt was particularly high at 77.8%, and AfD supporters in Magdeburg praised Siegmund's success in winning over voters.One man called Ollie said: "This man gives us what no-one else can give.""No matter what government, they all just promise things to get better. This is a party for the working people. It is the alternative for Germany," he told the BBC.Another AfD voter called Bert said people in the east could sense things were not going well: "Things need to improve for us, for my family - I have three children. I'm in fear, I'm really in fear that safety erodes more and more."Other parties refuse to go into coalition with the AfD, operating a Brandmauer or firewall aimed at keeping the far right out of government. In Saxony-Anhalt, the BSW has offered to co-operate with the AfD on some issues if it gets into the state parliament.The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states. They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally. It would not be able to achieve either if it ran the government of one of 16 states.But it would have significant local powers. The party has been particularly critical of the Bauhaus school of design which the Nazis shut down in the city of Dessau in Saxony-Anhalt after they came to power in 1933. The AfD has called it "the dead-end of modernism", prompting some to accuse the party of using similar language to the Nazis.Nikita, a demonstrator at an anti-AfD "Democracy Festival" in Magdeburg on the eve of the vote said Germans had to "learn from our history and not go back. We don't want the dark times any more".Responding to the news from Saxony-Anhalt, the veteran head of the Jewish community in Munich and Bavaria, Charlotte Knobloch, said it frightened her. "On days like this I find it hard to recognise my homeland any more," the 93-year-old Holocaust survivor said, appealing for mainstream parties not to stand by and allow "this decline".One of the AfD's top figures in Saxony-Anhalt, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, has also been criticised for his approach to Russia. When asked why he had a Russian army mug in his office, he said it was just a souvenir, and "it's not our war".

schema.headline: Germany's far-right AfD hails big victory in east, but falls short of majority

title: Australians will be able to switch off social media algorithms under planned legislation
description: Australians would be able to switch off social media algorithms under draft legislation to be proposed this week.Communications Minister Anika Wells,
body: Australians would be able to switch off social media algorithms under draft legislation to be proposed this week.Communications Minister Anika Wells, who last year helmed the government's world-first social media ban for under-16s, said the digital duty of care laws would ensure "some basic safety protections on an industry that hasn't had to observe it".If tech firms such as Meta, Google and TikTok did not give the option to turn off algorithms, they should face "substantial" penalties, she said.Some members of the opposition have criticised the proposal, with Liberal Party leader Angus Taylor saying he was "highly sceptical" and arguing the move could amount to censorship.The government will be taking "expert advice" on whether users would have to opt in or out of the algorithms feeding them content online, Wells said.This means that, as with its social media ban, the government is looking to bring in legislation before fully hammering out the specifics of how it would work."We want to give Australians more choice over what they see on their social media feeds," Wells told the ABC on Monday."We know that a lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm both for the enjoyment they get out of it or the utility that they get out of it, seeing local businesses in their suburb."A lot of Australians will want to choose the algorithm. But we think that big tech should offer them the choice in the first place and they should respect that choice."Big tech is not a protected species and they should offer their customers basic safety standards."But she admitted that so far no tech firm had been fined for not enforcing the social media ban, despite research consistently showing that the vast majority of under 16s who were on platforms before the ban was introduced last December, still use them.Some members of the opposition have said they support the idea in principle, but others argue it is an attempt to curtail freedom of speech. Taylor told News24 he feared this was "an attempt by the government to censor social media" and that Labor should first try to plug holes in the social media ban.Speaking to Channel Nine's Today show, Wells said: "This isn't about censorship. This is about identifying risks or making big tech identify the risks on their own platform and making big tech mitigate against those risks on their platform."Last week, high-profile consent advocate Chanel Contos gave a speech at Australia's National Press Club calling on the government to seek an opt-in for algorithmic social media feeds, making it harder for tech firms to find a way round any reforms.She argued algorithms were fuelling the prevalence of sexual violence in Australia and exposing young people to misogynistic "manosphere" material.The draft legislation is expected to be introduced in the coming days.  As well as addressing algorithms, it is also expected to put an onus on platforms to stop harmful content, such as illegal pornography and videos promoting disordered eating, from being shared.

schema.headline: Australians will be able to switch off social media algorithms under planned legislation

title: Peace talks rich in symbolism but differences between Russia and Ukraine remain
description: Image source, ReutersByDiplomatic correspondentThe talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian
body: Image source, ReutersByDiplomatic correspondentThe talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian soil for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion. The fact they had to travel by train because they could not risk flying and running the gauntlet of Russian drones - weapons launched on the orders of the man at whose table they sat in the Kremlin only hours ago. The symbolism of Ukrainian President Zelensky greeting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at Kyiv's Saint Sophia Cathedral, not only an icon of Ukraine's ancient history, but also just a few yards from where Russian drones hit the headquarters of the country's security services on Friday. You did not have to join too many dots to work out the point Zelensky was making.Both sides held talks for several hours; they were later joined by some European national security advisers, including the UK's National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell. And afterwards, all sides spoke warmly of having held substantive discussions. They spoke hopefully of reviving past "trilateral talks" involving both the US and Europe.Image source, ReutersBut fundamental differences remain. The US envoys had come hot foot from Moscow where Vladimir Putin had told them Russia was making "tangible advances" on the battlefield. The story they heard from Ukraine was different, in fact the opposite. Ukrainian officials claim that in August they gained more territory than they lost and Russia suffered 42,000 casualties, dead or wounded.Putin had also told the US envoys the root causes of the conflict had to be addressed, shorthand for his longstanding strategic demands that Ukraine cede territory, abandon hopes of joining Nato and reduce the size of its army.After the talks, Zelensky insisted Ukraine would require "strong and clear" security guarantees, including a strong army. Nor did he give any sign of being willing to give up any territory in the eastern Donbas region, an issue he described dryly as "difficult".Figure caption, Watch: President Zelensky welcomes US envoys in KyivWitkoff insisted progress had been made and the ingredients for a settlement were there. But he admitted both sides would have to make compromises to narrow the differences between them. And right now, it is hard to see either side doing that.So for now, the expectation in Kyiv is that the fighting will continue and they will face a hard winter ahead. Some diplomats talk of a window of opportunity for a possible settlement next spring. Others are less optimistic. Zelensky thanked the US envoys for their visit because the short-term pause in air strikes agreed by both sides had given the people of Kyiv a brief respite. Few expect it to last for long.Figure caption, Watch: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner say they are "encouraged" by Ukraine talks

schema.headline: Peace talks rich in symbolism but differences between Russia and Ukraine remain

title: Smaller ball in women's rugby: England players give verdict
description: England will play Australia, Canada and New Zealand in the next three weeks and, like all the world's top women's players, they have some new equipmen
body: England will play Australia, Canada and New Zealand in the next three weeks and, like all the world's top women's players, they have some new equipment: a smaller ball.During September and October's WXV Global Series, World Rugby is trialling a size 4.5 ball - about 3% smaller than the size five used in the men's game, but the same weight.Their introduction has not been without controversy and for England hooker May Campbell, responsible for throwing the ball in at the line-out, told BBC Sport it can go "a bit skew-whiff".One of England's kickers, Helena Rowland, has found a much bigger margin for error with the smaller ball, saying: "If you get it slightly wrong, the difference is massive."The fly-half says England players have noticed passes "dying", falling to the floor earlier than expected, "which they wouldn't have done previously".Not all feedback has been negative. Wales wing Lisa Neumann is a fan, saying "it's changed the game" for her passing because of improved grip on the ball.The thinking behind the trial is that the smaller ball will suit women's physiology and improve their skillset. In other sports, like basketball, women use a smaller ball, and in athletics sprint hurdles are lower for females.But Rowland says she has never felt "hindered" by playing with the same size ball as in men's rugby.Players with a specific skillset may find the change harder than others. Hookers must throw in at a line-out, scrum-halves are the most frequent passers and fly-halves the most regular kickers.Rowland explained: "We've learned for however long how to kick with a size five."So I've had 13-odd years of doing that and training my routine and trying to nail that and get as much consistency as I can."So it's about, I suppose, trying to pack all those years of training and all those kicks into a four- or five-week block to get used to it, to then go out on to the world stage."Rowland added that she has not "necessarily seen any positives", saying: "I know some of the girls have said that from an offload perspective, it's maybe made them more confident."But for me, it hasn't. I don't think there's enough of a change in the ball for me to be able to be running around with it in one hand and offloading left, right and centre."I haven't necessarily found any of the positive impacts. I've just found it a bit harder to do my job."A World Rugby spokesperson said everyone involved in the WXV Global Series, including players, coaches and match officials, would have their views taken into account "with equal value" through surveys.One area of concern for the England players is the ball changing shape.Campbell says they "played around" with how much the ball was blown up, adding: "In previous weeks it was actually a bit fatter, and then this week it definitely feels smaller."Rowland agrees, saying: "There needs to be a bit more done in terms of how the balls are made. We had some new balls today versus the ones we've had for the last three weeks [and the difference] is massive."If you've been training with an old ball that's fat to then go into a game and it's a completely different shape, actually that makes a massive difference as well, which I think is something that you don't necessarily find so much in the size five."The ball has already been trialled in the Under-18s and Under-20s Women's Six Nations as well as the HSBC Sevens Series.Rowland says she would "love to see the data on if it actually has made a difference".It seems a fair request, and is one that BBC Sport put to World Rugby, but we did not receive any data.A spokesperson said: "The balls haven't been used in the international XVs environment yet so there isn't directly comparable data to share with players either directly or via their unions."Once we've built up a large enough data set of player responses, match official responses and game data, we'll publish the results, so it'll be available to players, unions, the International Rugby Players Association, coaches, match officials, the media and everyone else."Some players are frustrated as they feel they have become guinea pigs on the global stage. To compound that frustration, they will then return to their clubs where the league season will be played with a size five ball once again.BBC Sport asked World Rugby when the trial period is likely to conclude, and were told: "We'll be able to assess our position on women's 15s once the international window has started. "This will allow for completion of the WXV tournaments and full analysis in early 2027. The evidence to date suggests that further exposure produces greater results."While it looks like players and coaches will get to see the data in early 2027, any wider outcomes or decisions might take longer.

schema.headline: Smaller ball in women's rugby: England players give verdict

title: Joshua vs Fury: Tyson Fury says he is looking for new opponent and calls out Oleksandr Usyk
description: Tyson Fury claims he is looking for a new opponent for November and has called out Oleksandr Usyk despite being contracted to fight Anthony Joshua nex
body: Tyson Fury claims he is looking for a new opponent for November and has called out Oleksandr Usyk despite being contracted to fight Anthony Joshua next.The all-British heavyweight showdown is being targeted for November, with both Joshua and Fury signing individual contracts for the contest.But the issue of where the fight takes place has caused a delay in an official announcement with organisers pushing to stage it in the US rather than Joshua's preferred location of Wembley Stadium.In an expletive-laden video posted on Instagram, Fury claimed Joshua was backing out of the fight."This will only lead me to a fight with Oleksandr Usyk," he said."Oleksandr you're his [Joshua's] trainer and his sensei and you know he is weak minded... and that he would never fight the Gypsy King which you have had the guts to do twice."You got the decisions last time, fair play to you. "Good luck to you, let's do it again. Let's run it back in November. The ball is now in your court... do you want to fight me this year, 2026, or are you calling it quits? "Let me know because I am now looking for a new opponent."Fury has twice lost to Usyk, with the two-time undisputed heavyweight champion now working with Joshua as part of his training and coaching team.Sela, Queensberry and Matchroom declined to comment on whether talks had broken down when contacted by BBC Sport.Saudi Arabian promoter Sela is fronting the bill for the prospective Joshua-Fury fight, with both men signing separate contracts with the company.Joshua's contract stipulates it must take place in the UK, leading to his promoter Eddie Hearn renegotiating details in that deal.But after London Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan made a public plea for the fight to happen at Wembley, Hearn said talks about staging it in the UK had "re-opened".Sela and broadcaster Netflix are understood to favour New York's Madison Square Garden.BBC Sport understands Sela has contacted the London mayor's office in recent weeks about bringing the long-awaited contest to the national stadium, but have not progressed talks further since last week.Hearn had said he hoped an announcement could happen in the coming week, but that now seems unlikely given the latest developments. A bout at Wembley may need to happen in the early hours - which would draw in a larger television audience in the US.Khan says his team would back such a proposal."A message to the promoters - we want to host it in London. Talk to us, we're really keen to have it," Khan told BBC Sport on Thursday."I'm hoping the promoters understand that not only will you get 100,000 people watching this bout live, you'll get millions watching it across the globe, where both boxers are cheered on by their loyal fans."

title: US Open 2026 results: Carlos Alcaraz beats Tommy Paul to reach quarter-finals
description: Carlos Alcaraz continued his return from long-term injury with a hugely impressive fourth-round win against Tommy Paul at the US Open.Playing just his
body: Carlos Alcaraz continued his return from long-term injury with a hugely impressive fourth-round win against Tommy Paul at the US Open.Playing just his fourth competitive singles match after an absence of more than four months, the 23-year-old Spaniard produced a masterful performance to beat American 20th seed Paul 6-4 6-3 6-4.He has dropped only one set on his way to the last eight in New York and will face American eighth seed Ben Shelton in the quarter-finals.A wrist injury caused Alcaraz to miss both the French Open and Wimbledon earlier this summer.He had won the previous two Grand Slams - last year's US Open and this year's Australian Open - meaning the straight-set victory over Paul extended his run of match wins at the majors to 18.Alcaraz is taking a different approach to this tournament in New York, putting a greater emphasis on recovery as he looks to keep his wrist injury-free - even if that means giving up his favourite off-court activity on his days off."I've been really focused on the recovery with my team, with myself, doing the right things off the court trying to be healthy and in good shape for the next round," he said."Those days, if I'm practising or not, I'm trying to be chill and focus on the next round. So golf this year isn't an option."Alcaraz has won all three of his tour-level matches against Shelton, who beat Stefanos Tsitsipas 6-2 6-3 6-4 later on Sunday."If Shelton were to come through, he is the kind of player that can knock the racquet out of your hand," said American former player Jeff Tarango on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra."It's going to be a real test to see how Alcaraz's wrist is with a 149mph serve coming to that forehand, but Alcaraz should get through Shelton if his wrist is fine."Later on Sunday, Frances Tiafoe, Alex Michelsen and Shelton stormed into the quarter-finals to boost home hopes of a first American men's Grand Slam champion since Andy Roddick won in New York in 2003.Tiafoe delighted fans in a entertaining victory over 2021 champion Daniil Medvedev, saving a set point in the third-set tie-break before wrapping up a 7-6 (7-1) 6-4 7-6 (8-6) win to maintain his perfect record on Louis Armstrong Stadium.Tiafoe has now won all 10 of his matches on the US Open's secondary show court, while it is just his second win in eight appearances against Russian Medvedev.A two-time semi-finalist in New York, Tiafoe will face Michelsen next after the 22-year-old beat Argentina's Tomas Martin Etcheverry 7-6 (8-6) 6-4 6-4 to reach his first Grand Slam quarter-final.Shelton, meanwhile, surged past Tsitsipas in less than two hours to join his compatriots in the last eight.Former world number three Tsitsipas had been enjoying a resurgence at Flushing Meadows as he defeated Arthur Fils and Jiri Lehecka, the 10th and 18th seeds, en route to his first fourth-round appearance at a Grand Slam in over two years.Tsitsipas' defeat means this is the first year a player with a one-handed backhand has not reached a major semi-final in men's singles since 1877.In the men's doubles, Britain's Henry Patten and Finnish team-mate Harri Heliovaara, the top seeds, moved into the third round with a 7-5 6-2 win over Matteo Arnaldi of Italy and Germany's Jan-Lennard Struff.British ninth seeds Lloyd Glasspool and Julian Cash won 7-6 (7-2) 6-4 against Czech pair Adam Pavalsek and Patrik Rikl, while Joe Salisbury and American partner Rajeev Ram fought back to beat French duo Theo Arribage and Albano Olivetti 6-7 (2-7) 7-6 (11-9) 6-4.

title: Indonesia volcano eruption leaves 270,000 stranded as airports extend closure
description: Snaking queues formed at the departure halls in Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Monday as stranded passengers sought refunds and tri
body: Snaking queues formed at the departure halls in Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Monday as stranded passengers sought refunds and tried to get updates on when they would be able to fly.Finna, who was supposed to fly home to Jakarta from Malang, a city in East Java, on Sunday morning, described the frezny at the airport as flights got repeatedly rescheduled."It was very crowded because passengers from the morning flights had piled up, while those scheduled for later departures still didn't know what would happen," the 46-year-old told BBC Indonesian. "We were all glued to the flight information screens."Not wanting to deal with the uncertainty, Finna eventually spent the night on two intercity trains before arriving in Jakarta at 03:00 on Monday."Everyone seems to be racking their brains [figuring alternative transportation options]", said Jo Shaw, who was visiting Indonesia with members of her conservation charity Save the Rhino International. Shaw's team had axed their plans to camp out at Java's Ujung Kulon National Park after authorities raised its alert level for the Anak Krakatau volcano."Being stranded in an airport hotel is a relatively minor inconvenience to be resolved in a few days hopefully," Shaw said, adding that she was more concerned about the teams working on the ground with the rhinos under such environmental conditions.A newly wed Malaysian couple who had just spent a week in Bali said they were told that the next flight back to Kuala Lumpur wouldn't be until 11 September."What are we going to do here for another five days? We only prepared enough money for our honeymoon and [were supposed] to go home yesterday," Amir Hamzah told Malaysia's national news agency Bernama."We thought we would just sleep at the airport for a few hours and then take the morning flight home [on Monday]. We never thought we would end up being stuck here for days," the 29-year-old said.On Monday, Indonesia's Geological Agency warned that "the probability of further eruptions in the coming periods remains high".Volcanic ash reached as high as 6,000m on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000m on the Sumatra side and in some parts of Java's westernmost province Banten, the meteorological agency BMKG said.Anak Krakatau sits on the Sunda Strait about midway between the islands of Java and Sumatra.The most recent eruption occurred at 20:23 on Sunday, according to the agency."We ‌cannot ascertain when this ‌will end due to the dynamic weather," Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said in relation to the temporary closures of the affected airports.Dudy said on Sunday that authorities across the airports have been conducting tests every 30 minutes "to anticipate whether the ash spread is widening or subsiding".Authorities have warned against approaching or engaging in activities within a 3km radius from the active crater, while ships passing through the Sunda Strait have also been prohibited from entering an exclusion zone of 3km radius from it.Authorities have also confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano.Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.The volcano collapsed in December 2018 triggering a huge tsunami which killed over 400 people, and displaced and injured thousands more on the nearby coastlines of Sumatra and Java.Scientists found that some of the chunks of rock that slid from the volcano when it collapsed were about 70-90m high.The Pacific Ring of Fire refers to a string of volcanoes, earthquake sites and tectonic plates around the Pacific. It spreads across 40,000km (25,000 miles) from the southern tip of South America all the way to New Zealand.Roughly 90% of all earthquakes occur along the area and the ring is dotted with 75% of all active volcanoes on Earth, that's 452 individual active volcanoes.With reporting by Farida Susanty in Jakarta and Koh Ewe in Singapore

title: Five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport
description: Figure caption, Watch: Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airportByMax Matza and Rafael Rojasat Miami International AirportUpdated 1 hour agoAn Amazo
body: Figure caption, Watch: Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airportByMax Matza and Rafael Rojasat Miami International AirportUpdated 1 hour agoAn Amazon Air cargo plane overshot the runway while attempting to land at Miami International Airport, killing five people and seriously injuring five more.The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft crashed just before 14:00 local time (19:00 GMT) after departing from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The flight also hit several vehicles on the ground.Amazon said that it is "working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened".All flights were ordered grounded by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) as fire crews raced to the smoking crash site. The crash comes over Labor Day weekend, one of the busiest travel times of the year.It is not yet clear whether those who died were in the plane, on the ground, or both."At least five people have lost their lives, and five others are injured," Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said at a news conference on Sunday evening.She added that rescue crews arrived at the scene within "seconds" of the crash. "Right now, our focus is on the families, those who were injured, and the ongoing response," she continued.Three of the five people injured are in critical condition, said Miami Fire Chief Raied Jadallah. The mayor said they were all taken to hospital with "unknown injuries".Several of the injured were trapped inside or under vehicles on the ground, and needed to be extricated by fire and rescue crews, said Jadallah.Officials say it is too early to know the cause of the crash, and that it will be investigated by the National Transportation Safety Board. The federal agency, which investigates all air crashes in the US, plans to hold a news conference on Monday. Image source, Getty ImagesThe Amazon flight operated by 21 Air, a charter company based in North Carolina, "overran Miami International Airport's diagonal runway and is disabled at the northwest end of the airport," the airport said in a statement.Miami Dade Fire Rescue said crews "arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing".Over 200 firefighters responded to the crash. The flames were extinguished, but there was still a fuel leak at the site, said Jadallah.Locals described the aftermath of the incident. One woman, Beth Tilman, told the New York Times said she had seen a black cloud where the plane had crashed, and had smelled an acrid stench. "It wasn't trees burning. It wasn't mangroves burning. It was some other odour that I, honestly, had never smelled before," she said.A student pilot, Rohan Ellis, told the same newspaper he had witnessed sirens and helicopters overhead when he arrived at the scene of the crash. Describing what had happened to the vehicles that the plane had hit, he said: "They were mangled."Amazon issued a statement saying that it was working closely with authorities and offering condolences to the victims. "We're heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today's incident at Miami International Airport," said Kelly Nantel, Amazon's Director of Corporate Global Media Relations."Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss."The airplane, which was operated by 21 Air, was attempting to land when this incident occurred. We're working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation."The BBC has emailed 21 Air about the incident, but has not received a response.Flight data from tracking site FlightRadar24 shows that the Amazon cargo flight was travelling at 112 knots (129mph, 207km/h) as it exited the "useable runway".In a blog post, the site says the plane came to rest near a parking lot that services an Amazon warehouse and other businesses.There were light thunderstorms and gusting winds in Miami at the time of the incident, the site says.Figure caption, 'Incredibly difficult day' Miami-Dade mayor says after five confirmed deadThe crash comes during one of the busiest travel weekends of the year in the US.Passengers at Miami International Airport told the BBC they were frustrated by the lack of information coming from officials, with many flights cancelled or delayed as a result of the incident. There were long lines at airline counters as people tried to reschedule travel plans, with some saying they would be forced to stay in Miami an extra night."The earliest I could find to fly to San Francisco was Tuesday morning," said one traveller named Faroush. "I'll probably have to find a hotel and spend more time in Miami."The Transportation Safety Administration (TSA) said there would be 17 million travellers passing through US airports in the week leading up to Monday's Labor Day holiday.The TSA, which screens passengers flying in the US, predicted that 2.3 million people would fly on Sunday alone.Miami International Airport (MIA) is located near downtown Miami, and is one of the busiest airports in the country."Founded in 1928, MIA is America's busiest airport for international freight and second busiest for international passengers, offers more flights to Latin America and the Caribbean than any other US airport," according to its website.About 60% of all international visitors to Florida arrive at this airport, it says.Did you witness the incident? Get in touch by clicking this link or use the form below. Get in touchDid you witness the crash? If you are able to do so, please get in touch.

title: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea: Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard shine for Gunners
description: Arsenal shelled out close to £200m on new signings during the summer transfer window but fell short of landing the elite forward they craved.Former Ma
body: Arsenal shelled out close to £200m on new signings during the summer transfer window but fell short of landing the elite forward they craved.Former Manchester City goalscorer Julian Alvarez was on their radar but remains at Atletico Madrid, while the Gunners were also interested in Aston Villa's Morgan Rogers, Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola and Vinicius Jr.While Rogers opted for London rivals Chelsea, Barcola moved to Liverpool and Vinicius Jr has stayed at Real Madrid.Yet reigning champions Arsenal have started this season as strongly as they finished 2025-26, when they celebrated their first Premier League title for 22 years.After wins over Coventry City and Aston Villa, they came from behind to beat big-spending Chelsea 2-1 in a thrilling derby on Sunday - thanks to goals from two familiar faces.Kai Havertz, an Arsenal player since 2023, and Martin Odegaard, who joined in 2021, scored as they passed their first big test of the campaign against opponents who have spent close to £350m since the end of last season.A maximum nine points from three games, one goal conceded and big players stepping up."I can't see anyone stopping Arsenal," former Premier League winner Chris Sutton told BBC Sport.It is surely too early in the season to get carried away, and there are likely to be bigger tests ahead for Mikel Arteta's side.But Arsenal have set down an early marker as they chase back-to-back Premier League crowns.Along with Manchester City, they are one of only two clubs with a maximum nine points from three games.After sweeping aside Coventry on the opening day of the season, they produced a mature performance to come away with all three points at Villa.Against Chelsea, they had to find a different way to win after £117m signing Rogers fired Chelsea into a second-minute lead."Our mentality is to keep fighting. We have shown that many times," said captain Odegaard, who scored the 50th-minute winner after Havertz had equalised before half-time."We never want to concede early, but the reaction is top. We got our reward in the end and the response was brilliant."We showed our quality with and without the ball and the result reflects that."Odegaard has scored three goals in four appearances in all competitions this season, after netting only once in 36 last term."It was a big game, massive game, tough opponent, and we got there in the end, so brilliant," he said.Former Manchester United and England player Ashley Young said Odegaard's form will be key for Arsenal this season."He's just a joy to watch," Young told BBC Sport."He's exciting when he gets on the ball, he's allowing other players to get on the ball."The connection down the right side between him, Bukayo Saka and Havertz - it's just good to see when you've got players that know each other and build relationships in that way."Riccardo Calafiori has been brilliant from last season. He seems to me like he's the one that's got a free role in the team."It was his run, and he played it precisely, for the winning goal. He goes quickly, takes people out of the way. It's just clever. Arsenal deserved all three points."Havertz said Odegaard was back to his "very best"."He's an unbelievable player - we have seen that over the last years," said the Germany forward."He's going to help us a lot this season."Sutton said Arsenal are still ahead of the rest, despite their rivals spending hundreds of millions of pounds during the transfer window."They're such a powerhouse," said the former Blackburn and England striker."Chelsea are a good team, but Arsenal always find a way to win. Can you stop Arsenal? I don't think they [other Premier League teams] can."Arsenal have won their opening three games of a top-flight campaign while conceding fewer than two goals (1) for the third time - after 1924-25, when they finished 20th, and 2003-04, when they went the season unbeaten.They have also won eight league games in a row stretching back to last season.Having seen off big-spending Chelsea, their next league match is at Sunderland on Saturday.Before that Arsenal launch their Champions League campaign at Napoli on Wednesday.Havertz said Arsenal will head to Italy with confidence high with after seeing off his former club Chelsea."Chelsea have an amazing squad, but so do we," said Havertz, who scored the winning goal for the Blues against Manchester City in the 2021 Champions League final."We knew it was going to be tough. They scored early, so it's not easy for us, but we believed in ourselves and changed the game around."

schema.headline: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea: Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard shine for Gunners

title: Zhenhao Zou could face more assault charges as Met hands file to CPS
description: A convicted serial rapist described by police as "one of the most prolific predators" in the UK could face further charges after fresh allegations inv
body: A convicted serial rapist described by police as "one of the most prolific predators" in the UK could face further charges after fresh allegations involving seven more women were passed to prosecutors.Chinese national Zhenhao Zou is serving a life sentence with a minimum term of 24 years after he was found guilty of drugging and raping 10 women in London and China between September 2019 and May 2023.Believing Zou had committed further crimes, police appealed for more potential victim-survivors to come forward.The Metropolitan Police has sent a file containing the new allegations of sexual crimes to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which will decide whether to bring further charges.According to the Met Police, the file contains evidence relating to several alleged offences, including rape and administering a substance with intent to commit a sexual offence.It relates to reports made by five women who contacted police following the appeal, as well as the alleged rape of two women who remain unidentified, the force said.A total of 23 women contacted police following the appeal, but most of them did not want to pursue criminal charges, the force added.The Met said separate inquiries were ongoing into allegations involving women who were allegedly assaulted by Zou in China, with officers working to obtain evidence from the Chinese authorities.

title: Indonesia fires: The volunteer firefighters risking their lives to defuse 'carbon bombs'
description: The volunteers risking their lives to defuse Indonesia's wildfire 'carbon bombs'Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Fahrin Ramadhianto has
body: The volunteers risking their lives to defuse Indonesia's wildfire 'carbon bombs'Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Fahrin Ramadhianto has been fighting Borneo's wildfires for a month - and noticing the impacts on his body.ByGavin Butler and Ahmad DhaniReporting fromBanjarbaru, KalimantanThe sky grows heavy in Borneo, though not with rain. The air, amber-hued and treacle-thick, is smudged under a blanket of smog that has spilled across international borders – to Singapore, Manila, Kuala Lumpur. Down on the ground, smoke steams from the soil.It's like tear gas, says Dwi Sujatmoko."It hits your nose straight away, your eyes burn – that's more or less what it's like," he says. "People say these fires are extraordinary because of the flames and the smoke. And they're right."The 35-year-old volunteer firefighter has spent more than a month enveloped in this haze, breathing toxic millennia-old microparticles of carbon as he toils against a seemingly inextinguishable fire front.Using hand tools, carts and portable fire pumps, he and thousands of other volunteer firefighters – many of them indigenous Dayak or Banjar people – are up against an inferno that has carbonised some 200,000 hectares of forest and farmland across Indonesian Borneo since early July. Underground and out of sight, giant subterranean peat fires continue to smoulder, choking the air with poisonous fumes."Once a fire becomes uncontrolled, it harms many people. Not just humans, but also animals and plants," Sujatmoko says. "If underground fire spreads and can no longer be controlled, the losses are enormous."Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Fires have torched some 200,000 hectares across Indonesian Borneo since early JulyIndonesia is in the throes of a wildfire catastrophe.Amid a so-called "Super El Niño" that has supercharged local drought conditions, thousands of active fire hotspots are spreading and multiplying across the country, fuelling a transnational haze crisis that is the region's worst in more than a decade.But what makes Borneo's fires particularly worrying is the fact that they are burning through one of the world's largest tropical peatland ecosystems.This 4.5-million-hectare swathe of forest and swamp, under normal conditions, serves as a valuable reservoir for ancient carbon.When these peatlands catch fire, they risk releasing millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane into the atmosphere – a "pulse" of greenhouse gas emissions that has earned them the sobriquet of "carbon bomb"."Peatlands are incredibly effective carbon stores because their waterlogged conditions slow decomposition, allowing carbon to accumulate underground for thousands of years," explains Dr Nisa Novita, a peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN)."But this also means they can become a 'carbon bomb' when they are drained or burned, because that carbon can be rapidly released into the atmosphere."Tropical peatlands in Indonesia are among the world's most effective natural carbon stores. The deeper the peat, the greater the carbon stock – and in Kalimantan, we have found peat deposits that can exceed 20 metres in depth."A peatland that deep has been known to harbour more than 6,000 tonnes of carbon – roughly equivalent to the annual CO₂ emissions of 4,800 cars – per hectare. And when it burns, says Dr Nisa, that fossilised carbon can be released into the atmosphere "very rapidly".Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, "We're doing everything we can to help deal with this haze disaster because it's our duty," says firefighter Dwi SujatmokoThe toxic cloudThousands of people across South East Asia are now feeling the effects of those emissions in their eyes, chests and throats. Across Indonesia as well as Brunei, Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines, air pollution indices have soared to "unhealthy" extremes - almost 75 times the World Health Organization's recommended level, in some cases – and hospital admissions have surged.Between July and August, Indonesia's Health Ministry recorded over 50,000 cases of respiratory infections linked to land and forest fires. More than 12,000 of them were children under the age of five."Everybody who's living within that pollution cloud is breathing in the products of those smouldering peat fires," says Susan Page, a professor at the University of Leicester's school of geology and the environment, who's been researching peatlands in Asia for three decades."They're breathing in carbon monoxide, which is toxic, and they're breathing in the very finely divided particulate matter... [which] can pass through the alveoli in the lungs into the bloodstream and cause further problems elsewhere in the body, including issues with the heart."Living in this kind of pollution cloud is extremely unhealthy."Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Fighting peat fires requires saturating the ground so thoroughly that it becomes "like porridge"Nowhere are these health impacts being felt more acutely than at the coalface of the disaster: the fire front.Here, volunteer firefighters have been risking their lives and lungs to extinguish burning peatlands which are notoriously difficult to put out. Two volunteers  in Central Kalimantan have died in recent days, reportedly after their health deteriorated from putting out fires.Cloaked in toxic haze that can burn years off a person's lifespan, volunteers have been digging ponds, canals and borewells through bone-dry peat in a desperate attempt to keep their hoses tapped. Some have been driving pipes into the earth, making ad hoc irrigation systems to combat subterranean fires. Others have been sleeping within a stone's throw of the frontline so they can battle the blazes through the night."The worst thing here has been the smoke," says Fahrin Ramadhianto, a volunteer firefighter in South Kalimantan's Banjarbaru, one of the worst-hit areas. "The smell is like decaying wood being burned – that's the characteristic smell of peat. And that peat contains decomposed wood and organic material from many different sources."An unnatural imbalanceIndonesia's peatland fires are not a new phenomenon. Experts say the crisis is rooted in decades of land-use change, dating back to the Suharto era, when vast areas of rainforest and peatland in Kalimantan were opened for logging, plantations and large-scale development projects.Yet authorities have historically avoided blaming industrial actors for causing large-scale fires. Instead, the same indigenous communities who are now engaged in firefighting operations across the island have often been accused of triggering the blazes, due to traditional farming methods that use controlled burns to clear away vegetation.Tono, a representative of the Dayak Kanayatn people of West Kalimantan, told the BBC that Dayak communities are frequently used as scapegoats, despite carrying out land clearing with extensive planning, caution and adherence to multi-generational customs. Tono says these communities' traditional practices, known as uma bukit or "hill farming", are rooted in the idea of maintaining balance with nature.Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, "The worst thing here has been the smoke," says Fahrin RamadhiantoBut the natural balance is fast unravelling in Kalimantan, the most deforested area in Indonesia. The region lost almost 160,000 hectares of forest area in 2025, more than one-third of the nationwide figure – much of it to make way for plantations and monocrop agriculture.It is these same industrial-scale development projects that have been largely responsible for draining the area's peat swamps, which renders them significantly more fire-prone, Prof Page says."Peatlands aren't really the ideal place to set up a plantation – but of course, once the more suitable mineral soils had been exhausted it became possible, by using large machinery, to drain the peatlands and create conditions which would be dry enough," she says."So not only have you got the deforestation, but peatland drainage of course has also greatly increased the fire risk."Page also points out that, whether on fire or not, a drained peatland emits carbon dioxide into the atmosphere "all of the time"."I think that's forgotten," she says. "I think it's important to recognise that when we see the fires, they're like a dramatic example of what is actually going on the whole time in a drained peatland... The fires are just the worst expression of [that]."Now, as these latest fires continue to spiral out of control, Sujatmoko and others face a concatenation of difficulties in the coming days, weeks and months – not least of which is a shortage of water. Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Drainage and drought in Indonesia's peatlands has exacerbated their vulnerability to fire Fighting peat fires requires saturating the ground so thoroughly that it becomes "like porridge", Sujatmoko explains.Even then there is a high chance the fire will reappear, like a smoking revenant, fed by hidden fuel buried in the invisible depths of the peat swamp.In the face of these persistent reignitions, ongoing drought conditions and toxic smog, fatigue is another concern."We're definitely tired," says Sujatmoko. "We get exhausted, we miss our families, our children, our wives. But for now, all of us are putting those things aside. We're doing everything we can to help deal with this haze disaster because it's our duty.""We also hope rain comes soon," he adds. "We've spent months away from home... May all the efforts of those on the front lines be a blessing for everyone."Additional reporting by Faisal Irfani from BBC Indonesian.

schema.headline: Indonesia fires: The volunteer firefighters risking their lives to defuse 'carbon bombs'
